Curious if there’s a known upper limit for that ingredient while using isotretinion. 
Jax is playing on two basketball teams now. Plus it’s June Ball here in AZ so he’s playing 2-3 games each day, so we want to keep his nutrient intake dialed without any contraindications with this new Rx regime. 
Hey [NAME],
Great to hear Jaxon is still at it! 1-tab of the Active/d (dose appropriate for 12-17yrs) only contains 375 mcg (1,250 IU) of vitamin A, which is not a large dose, and by itself is unlikely to cause a problem in a healthy 16/17-year-old taking the drug. The rest is provitamin A, beta carotene at 825 mcg/2750), which should be no issue. However, check with his dermatologist if that amount is ok. Otherwise, use another multivitamin and mineral formula (MVM) that only uses beta-carotene for vitamin A until he is finished with the Accutane/isotretinoin. Below from the Practitioner Dietary Supplement Reference Guide (PDSRG) on vitamin A in our Active.
Have a great day brother and let’s catch up soon!
Vitamin A: contains 1200 mcg (4000 IU) of vitamin A from both preformed vitamin A, retinol acetate (375 mcg/1250 IU) and provitamin A, beta carotene (825 mcg/2750) since they both metabolize differently with unique and mutual actions. However, partially attributed to genetics and other uptake factors,, there can be large interindividual differences in the ability to convert pro-vitamin A sources (e.g. alpha-carotene, beta-carotene, etc.) to the needed amount of vitamin A activity, known as retinol activity equivalents (RAE), therefore both forms can help offset the possibility of too much or too little vitamin A activity and potentially more accurately contribute to achieving the recommended levels.,, 
Hey [NAME]!
Jaxon started isotretinoin and we read that he should avoid retinoic acid (beta carotene may be okay). I noticed the ActiveMV has both for Vit A, with retinoic acid as the first listed ingredient.
Curious if there’s a known upper limit for that ingredient while using isotretinion. 
Jax is playing on two basketball teams now. Plus it’s June Ball here in AZ so he’s playing 2-3 games each day, so we want to keep his nutrient intake dialed without any contraindications with this new Rx regime. 
MORE INFO
is it ok for a 16yr old male taking isotretinoin for acne, to continue using his multivitamin that contains vitamin A, retinol acetate at 375 mcg/1250 IU, since it's not a high amount? 
The conservative medical answer is:
Most dermatologists recommend avoiding supplemental vitamin A while taking isotretinoin (Accutane), even if the amount is relatively small.
Here's why:
Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative (retinoid). 
Many of the side effects of isotretinoin are essentially signs of excess retinoid exposure. 
Combining isotretinoin with additional vitamin A can theoretically increase the risk of: 
Dry skin and lips 
Headaches 
Liver stress 
Elevated triglycerides 
Joint aches 
Rarely, vitamin A toxicity symptoms 
That said, your example contains:
375 mcg retinol acetate (1,250 IU vitamin A)
which is actually a fairly modest amount. For perspective:
RDA for a 16-year-old male = about 900 mcg RAE/day (~3,000 IU) 
Upper Limit (UL) for ages 14–18 = 2,800 mcg RAE/day (~9,300 IU) 
So the amount in the multivitamin by itself is not high.
Practical Consideration
If the dermatologist specifically said:
"Avoid vitamin A supplements"
then I would discontinue the multivitamin or switch to one without preformed vitamin A during treatment.
If the multivitamin is otherwise important and contains only:
375 mcg retinol acetate 
no additional vitamin A supplements 
no cod liver oil 
many physicians would not consider that amount a major concern, but it is still worth confirming with the prescribing dermatologist because they know:
the isotretinoin dose 
treatment duration 
liver enzyme results 
triglyceride levels 
What I Usually Recommend
For someone on isotretinoin:
✅ Continue:
Multivitamin without vitamin A if available 
Vitamin D 
Minerals 
Omega-3s 
Protein supplements 
⚠️ Avoid:
Additional vitamin A supplements 
High-vitamin A liver supplements 
Cod liver oil 
Acne products containing strong retinoids unless specifically prescribed 
Bottom Line
375 mcg (1,250 IU) of vitamin A is not a large dose, and by itself is unlikely to cause toxicity in a healthy 16-year-old. However, because isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative, the standard recommendation is to avoid supplemental vitamin A during treatment when practical. If the multivitamin is otherwise valuable, I would ask the prescribing dermatologist whether that specific amount is acceptable rather than assuming it is automatically safe.

source_file: 2026/Juan 150lbs Suppbesast.docx
filename: Juan 150lbs Suppbesast
expert_section:
Juan, before we get started on your answer:
Caveat to all numbers is the accuracy your numbers (e.g., calorie count, bodyfat, etc.,)- but it doesn’t matter, they are just numbers you have assigned to where you are today -or placeholders for a starting place. Because you have found your maintenance, so that is the spot we work from – the ongoing body fat directional changes and actual overall body composition numbers will capture the true results regardless of your numbers – i.e., we are looking at actual changes to measure progress so we can add, subtract, etc. to move in the right direction until we the goal).
Let Me Break This Down For You
First off — respect. Seriously. Losing 30 pounds since November, building substantial muscle, running a restaurant 4 days a week on 10-12 hour shifts, AND maintaining a structured morning routine with training? That's not a guy who lacks discipline. That's a guy who's hitting a very specific, very solvable problem.
Here's the thing — what you're experiencing is textbook metabolic adaptation, and the good news is we know exactly what's happening and what to do about it.
What's Actually Going On
At 150 lbs and 5'6", you're not a big guy. You've lost 30 lbs, built muscle, and your body has fully adapted to “1,400 calories” (or whatever your weekly average caloric intake is in the past weeks). That IS now your maintenance level. Your metabolism has slightly downregulated to match your intake including adapting to a lower body weight so you naturally burn less calories doing the same activities when you were at a higher body weight. It's not broken — it's actually doing exactly what it's designed to do. It protected you. Now we have to outsmart it.
The "stay the course" advice from your current coach? Look, I'm not here to throw anyone under the bus, but when the data is telling you something isn't working anymore, you don't just stay the course. You adjust. That's the whole game.
Your Numbers First
Let me give you some context here. At 150 lbs and roughly 20-25% body fat, you're carrying approximately: 112-120 lbs of lean body mass (LBM); 30-37 lbs of body fat
To get to 10% body fat, assuming you maintain or even add a little muscle, you're looking at getting down to roughly 125-130 lbs total weight — or building enough muscle that 10% body fat sits at a higher scale weight. Either way, you've got real work ahead, but it's absolutely achievable.
---
Here's My Breakdown — Step by Step
1. Stop Thinking About the Scale and Start Measuring Body Fat Every Two Weeks
The scale is lying to you right now. You said it yourself — you've gained substantial muscle. That muscle is probably masking some fat loss on the scale. Get a reliable body fat measurement method (DEXA if you can access it, or a good caliper protocol) and track that every two weeks. That's your real progress marker. Weight is almost meaningless at your stage.
2. You Need a Calorie Recalculation — But Probably NOT Another Cut
Here's where I'm going to push back on both camps — the "cut more" crowd AND the "just eat more" crowd. At 1,400 calories, you're already very low for a 50-year-old active male running a restaurant. Cutting further risks:
- Accelerated muscle loss
- Further metabolic suppression
- Hormonal disruption (especially important given your peptide protocol and DHEA use)
- Feeling like garbage, which tanks your performance and adherence
The bottom line is — you've established “1,400” as your new maintenance. The move isn't necessarily to drop to 1,100-1,200. That's a dangerous road at your size and activity level.
3. Strategic Calorie Cycling Is Your Next Move
This is what I'd look at seriously. Instead of a flat 1,400 every day, consider:
- Training days (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat): Bump to 1,600-1,700 calories, with the added calories coming from targeted carbohydrates around your workout window
- Non-training/restaurant work days (Wed, Fri, Sun): Keep at 1,300-1,400, staying lower carb/carnivore (lean proteins -but get some very low calorie veggies in) leaning.
This does two things — it gives your metabolism a signal that starvation isn't happening (preventing further adaptation), AND it puts fuel exactly where it needs to go: into your training. You're on a low-carb carnivore base, which can be fine, but on training days your muscles want glucose. Even a targeted 50-100g of quality carbs around your workout can meaningfully change your body composition trajectory and help your peptides work better.
4. Your Protein Needs to Be Non-Negotiable
At your LBM, you need at minimum 112-120 grams of protein daily, but ideally closer to 130-150 grams. On a carnivore-leaning 1,400 calorie diet, this is achievable but you need to be hitting it consistently. Protein is the most important macro for preserving and building muscle while in a deficit. It also has the highest thermic effect — your body burns more calories just digesting it.
Your dotFIT Aminos in the morning is a great start. Make sure you're counting that toward your total (2scoops can be counted as ~30gms in your case toward your daily total – but no more regardless of how much you use) . Get protein in at every meal or feeding opportunity.
5. Address the Metabolic Reset With a Short Diet Break
This is something the research supports strongly. After an extended period of caloric restriction (and you've been at this since November), your leptin drops, your thyroid slows, your metabolism adapts. A 1-2 week diet break at true maintenance — which for you might actually be 1,800-2,000 calories based on your activity — can partially restore metabolic rate before you re-enter a deficit. This isn't quitting. This is strategy.
6. Add NEAT — Your Restaurant Days Are Actually An Asset
Here's something people miss. You're on your feet 10-12 hours in a restaurant 4 days a week. That's significant non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). Make sure you're not unconsciously compensating by sitting more on your off days. On your off days, prioritize walking. Even 30-45 minutes of easy walking adds meaningful caloric expenditure without touching your recovery or muscle mass. Your rowing machine baseline is great for movement — keep that. But add deliberate walking on off days (use a Fit-Bit/phone or any step counter).
7. Your Training Needs a Progressive Overload Check
X3 bands to failure is solid. But here's my question — are you actually progressing? Meaning, is each session getting harder in some measurable way? More reps, longer time under tension, shorter rest periods, thicker bands? If you've been doing the same exercises at the same resistance for weeks, your body has adapted to that stimulus too. The muscle-building signal has to keep coming. Talk to your coach about how you're tracking progression in those movements.
8. Build a Proper Foundation With Your Supplement Stack
You've got some solid pieces in place — DHEA, D3+K, MTHF, creatine (excellent for body composition and strength at your age), and the peptides. But I want to make sure you've got a complete multivitamin/mineral formula locked in as your foundation. When you're in a caloric deficit, micronutrient gaps are real and they affect everything — energy, recovery, hormonal function, sleep.
I'd strongly recommend the dotFIT All-in-1 SuperBlend as your comprehensive multi base. At 50, in a deficit, training hard, running a restaurant — your micronutrient demands are high and your food variety may not be covering all the gaps, especially on a carnivore-leaning approach. The All-in-1 SuperBlend is designed for active people with serious goals and covers those bases properly alongside everything else you're doing. Take 1-scoop in the AM and one in the PM.
9. Consider Adding the dotFIT Weight Loss & Liver Support Stack
Here's something directly relevant to your situation. At your stage — pushing past a plateau toward a lean body composition goal — adding a liver support and fat metabolism product like dotFIT Weight Loss & Liver Support can be genuinely useful. Your liver is central to fat metabolism, and supporting it matters especially when you're coming off an extended deficit and working long restaurant days. Pair that with LeanMeal as a structured meal replacement to nail one or two of your daily feedings with precision — protein, fiber, controlled calories. It removes the guesswork on those busy restaurant days when you might grab whatever's available. Take 2-shakes daily added to 2- traditional food meals to help in calorie accuracy and daily energy levels.
10. Get Real Data With Consistent Tracking for the Next 30 Days
Before you make any big changes, spend the next 2-3 weeks doing one thing: tracking everything with precision. I mean everything. Use an app, weigh your food if you need to on days off, log honestly. You might think you're at 1,400, but restaurant environments are notorious for untracked bites, tastes, and samples. Once you have clean data, you'll know for certain what you're working with and can make a truly informed adjustment.
---
The Bottom Line for Juan
You've done the hard part — you've built a foundation of muscle that most guys your age haven't got. Now we're talking about precision, not punishment. The answer isn't just "eat less" or blindly. And finally, when we achieve the goal, the calories will go up to a new maintenance and the workload can be lessened so our calories out and in are stable.

Juan, before we get started on your answer:
Caveat to all numbers is the accuracy your numbers (e.g., calorie count, bodyfat, etc.,)- but it doesn’t matter, they are just numbers you have assigned to where you are today -or placeholders for a starting place. Because you have found your maintenance, so that is the spot we work from – the ongoing body fat directional changes and actual overall body composition numbers will capture the true results regardless of your numbers – i.e., we are looking at actual changes to measure progress so we can add, subtract, etc. to move in the right direction until we the goal).
Let Me Break This Down For You
First off — respect. Seriously. Losing 30 pounds since November, building substantial muscle, running a restaurant 4 days a week on 10-12 hour shifts, AND maintaining a structured morning routine with training? That's not a guy who lacks discipline. That's a guy who's hitting a very specific, very solvable problem.
Here's the thing — what you're experiencing is textbook metabolic adaptation, and the good news is we know exactly what's happening and what to do about it.
What's Actually Going On
At 150 lbs and 5'6", you're not a big guy. You've lost 30 lbs, built muscle, and your body has fully adapted to “1,400 calories” (or whatever your weekly average caloric intake is in the past weeks). That IS now your maintenance level. Your metabolism has slightly downregulated to match your intake including adapting to a lower body weight so you naturally burn less calories doing the same activities when you were at a higher body weight. It's not broken — it's actually doing exactly what it's designed to do. It protected you. Now we have to outsmart it.
The "stay the course" advice from your current coach? Look, I'm not here to throw anyone under the bus, but when the data is telling you something isn't working anymore, you don't just stay the course. You adjust. That's the whole game.
Your Numbers First
Let me give you some context here. At 150 lbs and roughly 20-25% body fat, you're carrying approximately: 112-120 lbs of lean body mass (LBM); 30-37 lbs of body fat
To get to 10% body fat, assuming you maintain or even add a little muscle, you're looking at getting down to roughly 125-130 lbs total weight — or building enough muscle that 10% body fat sits at a higher scale weight. Either way, you've got real work ahead, but it's absolutely achievable.
---
Here's My Breakdown — Step by Step
1. Stop Thinking About the Scale and Start Measuring Body Fat Every Two Weeks
The scale is lying to you right now. You said it yourself — you've gained substantial muscle. That muscle is probably masking some fat loss on the scale. Get a reliable body fat measurement method (DEXA if you can access it, or a good caliper protocol) and track that every two weeks. That's your real progress marker. Weight is almost meaningless at your stage.
2. You Need a Calorie Recalculation — But Probably NOT Another Cut
Here's where I'm going to push back on both camps — the "cut more" crowd AND the "just eat more" crowd. At 1,400 calories, you're already very low for a 50-year-old active male running a restaurant. Cutting further risks:
- Accelerated muscle loss
- Further metabolic suppression
- Hormonal disruption (especially important given your peptide protocol and DHEA use)
- Feeling like garbage, which tanks your performance and adherence
The bottom line is — you've established “1,400” as your new maintenance. The move isn't necessarily to drop to 1,100-1,200. That's a dangerous road at your size and activity level.
3. Strategic Calorie Cycling Is Your Next Move
This is what I'd look at seriously. Instead of a flat 1,400 every day, consider:
- Training days (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat): Bump to 1,600-1,700 calories, with the added calories coming from targeted carbohydrates around your workout window
- Non-training/restaurant work days (Wed, Fri, Sun): Keep at 1,300-1,400, staying lower carb/carnivore (lean proteins -but get some very low calorie veggies in) leaning.
This does two things — it gives your metabolism a signal that starvation isn't happening (preventing further adaptation), AND it puts fuel exactly where it needs to go: into your training. You're on a low-carb carnivore base, which can be fine, but on training days your muscles want glucose. Even a targeted 50-100g of quality carbs around your workout can meaningfully change your body composition trajectory and help your peptides work better.
4. Your Protein Needs to Be Non-Negotiable
At your LBM, you need at minimum 112-120 grams of protein daily, but ideally closer to 130-150 grams. On a carnivore-leaning 1,400 calorie diet, this is achievable but you need to be hitting it consistently. Protein is the most important macro for preserving and building muscle while in a deficit. It also has the highest thermic effect — your body burns more calories just digesting it.
Your dotFIT Aminos in the morning is a great start. Make sure you're counting that toward your total (2scoops can be counted as ~30gms in your case toward your daily total – but no more regardless of how much you use) . Get protein in at every meal or feeding opportunity.
5. Address the Metabolic Reset With a Short Diet Break
This is something the research supports strongly. After an extended period of caloric restriction (and you've been at this since November), your leptin drops, your thyroid slows, your metabolism adapts. A 1-2 week diet break at true maintenance — which for you might actually be 1,800-2,000 calories based on your activity — can partially restore metabolic rate before you re-enter a deficit. This isn't quitting. This is strategy.
6. Add NEAT — Your Restaurant Days Are Actually An Asset
Here's something people miss. You're on your feet 10-12 hours in a restaurant 4 days a week. That's significant non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). Make sure you're not unconsciously compensating by sitting more on your off days. On your off days, prioritize walking. Even 30-45 minutes of easy walking adds meaningful caloric expenditure without touching your recovery or muscle mass. Your rowing machine baseline is great for movement — keep that. But add deliberate walking on off days (use a Fit-Bit/phone or any step counter).
7. Your Training Needs a Progressive Overload Check
X3 bands to failure is solid. But here's my question — are you actually progressing? Meaning, is each session getting harder in some measurable way? More reps, longer time under tension, shorter rest periods, thicker bands? If you've been doing the same exercises at the same resistance for weeks, your body has adapted to that stimulus too. The muscle-building signal has to keep coming. Talk to your coach about how you're tracking progression in those movements.
8. Build a Proper Foundation With Your Supplement Stack
You've got some solid pieces in place — DHEA, D3+K, MTHF, creatine (excellent for body composition and strength at your age), and the peptides. But I want to make sure you've got a complete multivitamin/mineral formula locked in as your foundation. When you're in a caloric deficit, micronutrient gaps are real and they affect everything — energy, recovery, hormonal function, sleep.
I'd strongly recommend the dotFIT All-in-1 SuperBlend as your comprehensive multi base. At 50, in a deficit, training hard, running a restaurant — your micronutrient demands are high and your food variety may not be covering all the gaps, especially on a carnivore-leaning approach. The All-in-1 SuperBlend is designed for active people with serious goals and covers those bases properly alongside everything else you're doing. Take 1-scoop in the AM and one in the PM.
9. Consider Adding the dotFIT Weight Loss & Liver Support Stack
Here's something directly relevant to your situation. At your stage — pushing past a plateau toward a lean body composition goal — adding a liver support and fat metabolism product like dotFIT Weight Loss & Liver Support can be genuinely useful. Your liver is central to fat metabolism, and supporting it matters especially when you're coming off an extended deficit and working long restaurant days. Pair that with LeanMeal as a structured meal replacement to nail one or two of your daily feedings with precision — protein, fiber, controlled calories. It removes the guesswork on those busy restaurant days when you might grab whatever's available. Take 2-shakes daily added to 2- traditional food meals to help in calorie accuracy and daily energy levels.
10. Get Real Data With Consistent Tracking for the Next 30 Days
Before you make any big changes, spend the next 2-3 weeks doing one thing: tracking everything with precision. I mean everything. Use an app, weigh your food if you need to on days off, log honestly. You might think you're at 1,400, but restaurant environments are notorious for untracked bites, tastes, and samples. Once you have clean data, you'll know for certain what you're working with and can make a truly informed adjustment.
---
The Bottom Line for Juan
You've done the hard part — you've built a foundation of muscle that most guys your age haven't got. Now we're talking about precision, not punishment. The answer isn't just "eat less" or blindly. And finally, when we achieve the goal, the calories will go up to a new maintenance and the workload can be lessened so our calories out and in are stable.

A: Thanks for contacting us. Yes, all products are tested for lead and ours are far below federal and global set limits, which our 3rd party testing validates. You may use any of our proteins daily with no issues. For reference, a cup of natural fresh spinach has more lead than a serving our proteins. See below for more information.
Thanks again and enjoy your protein shakes as needed. 
More Info
First, all anyone needs is the 3rd Party/NSF testing verification on the labels because those official companies cannot certify a product that is over the federal set limit of any natural compounds/metals including lead.
And yes, all our proteins are well below global and federal standards and again, validated by our 3rd party testing (NSF-CS and Eurofins). We use news/articles like this to sell our proteins. Also be mindful that there is always some lead (and other natural metals found in the earth), including in the air you breathe, in natural products (see note), but there is a set limit that you cannot exceed, and the testing confirms that. Again, all our powders are far below the federal and global limits, which is verified by NSF-CS and Eurofins our 3rd and 4th party testing.
On a side note, 1svg of natural spinach has 10times the allowed lead in any dietary supplement. In other words, most plant foods will always be above the allowed lead content for dietary supplements, especially the artificially low California only standard. Just make sure your supplements are 3rd party tested like all of ours and you will always be safe.

Global demand for spirulina is booming, with the market for thissuperfood projected to reach $1.3 billion by 2032. But new testing revealed some cracks in quality and safety that suggest some top-selling products may expose consumers to elevated lead levels
Cyanotech conducted an initial screening of 37 top-selling spirulina and greensproducts, which were selected based in their “top-selling” status based on datafrom SPINS, Amazon sales and review volume, market visibility on Google andsocial listening. Subsequent third-party testing by Eurofins confirmed the presenceof lead in nearly half of the samples. The company then expanded the analysis to asecond phase, in which Alkemist Labs tested 19 products across multiple lots, witha greater focus on organic-labeled products.
Because spirulina is a bio-accumulator, it absorbs not only nutrients but also anycontaminants present in the water where it is cultivated. Since it is grown in aquaticsystems, the quality of that environment directly determines the ingredient’s purity.
“What makes this especially important is how spirulina is consumed. It is harvested,dried and delivered in a highly concentrated form,” Kakuk explained. “A singleserving of powder represents a large amount of original biomass, so everything in itis concentrated as well, including all the beneficial nutrients–but also any contaminants present.”

What Happens to Your Hormones When You Don’t Eat Enough Carbs
Key Takeaways:
Very low carbohydrate (carb) intake can shift blood sugar hormones in ways that may make energy feel less predictable.
Carb restriction may alter thyroid, serotonin, and reproductive hormones, affecting mood, metabolism, and menstrual cycle irregularity.
Appetite might decrease as your body adapts to a lower carb intake over time, due to increased leptin sensitivity and stable or decreased ghrelin levels.
When you cut carbs too low for your body’s needs, several hormones shift in an effort to keep you going. Some of these changes can be helpful in the short term, but over time, they may disrupt energy, mood, appetite, and blood sugar control.

source_file: 2026/MCL Tear rehab protocol .docx
filename: MCL Tear rehab protocol
expert_section:
Yes. For an isolated Grade 2 MCL tear (partial tear) with a stable knee and no associated ACL/meniscus injury, nonoperative treatment is standard, and the prognosis is generally excellent. The emphasis is early protected motion, progressive loading, restoring quadriceps/hamstring/hip strength, then balance and sport-specific function—not prolonged immobilization. 
A practical protocol would look something like this:
| Phase | Approx. timing | Main goals & activities |
| 1. Protect & calm it down | Days 0–7 | Hinged MCL brace if recommended; weight-bear as tolerated, crutches if limping; ice/compression/elevation; avoid valgus stress, twisting and pivoting. Begin gentle heel slides, quad sets, straight-leg raises and comfortable knee ROM. |
| 2. Restore motion & basic strength | Weeks 1–3 | Progress toward normal walking and full extension/flexion. Stationary bike with little/no resistance. Quad sets, SLRs, hamstring curls, calf raises, bridges, hip abduction/adduction as tolerated, partial squats and light leg press. Start basic single-leg balance. |
| 3. Rebuild strength & stability | Weeks 3–6 | Progress squats, leg press, step-ups/step-downs, split squats/lunges, hamstring work, calf raises and hip/glute strengthening. Increase cycling/elliptical. Progress single-leg balance and proprioception. Still be cautious with aggressive lateral/cutting movements. |
| 4. Return to athletic movement | ~Weeks 4–8+ | Once walking, stairs and strength work are pain-free with no swelling: progress jogging → running → lateral movement → agility → plyometrics → sport-specific drills. Grade 2 athletes may undergo functional testing around 6–8 weeks. |
What I would emphasize
During the first 1–2 weeks, I wouldn't try to "test" the MCL repeatedly with side-to-side movements. The ligament needs some protection while it heals. A short hinged brace is commonly used, particularly when walking; Mass General's protocol describes bracing for roughly 3–6 weeks depending on severity, although individual sports-medicine practices vary considerably. 
At the same time, you generally don't want to shut the leg down completely. As pain and swelling permit, regain knee motion and maintain quad activation. Mass General includes quad sets, heel slides, straight-leg raises, short-arc extensions, hamstring curls, calf raises, hip abduction, partial squats and wall slides in its MCL program. 
A simple strength progression
Once ordinary walking is comfortable, I'd think of the progression as:
Bike → bilateral squat/leg press → step-ups → split squat → single-leg squat/step-down → dynamic balance → jogging → lateral movement → cutting/agility.
The important point is that progression should be criteria-based rather than simply calendar-based. Don't advance because "it's week 4"; advance because the knee has demonstrated that it can handle the previous workload.
For full return to sport, a good target is full ROM, essentially no pain, no swelling after exercise, no instability, and ≥90% quadriceps/hamstring/hip strength and functional performance compared with the other leg. Those are also essentially Sanford's return-to-sport criteria. 
One particularly important point for golf
If this is related to the golfer/MCL situation we've been discussing, golf is interesting because walking and straight-line strengthening can return relatively early, while the rotational forces of the golf swing should come later. I would separate "return to exercise" from "return to golf."
A sensible progression would be putting → chipping → short pitches → half swings → ¾ swings → full irons → driver → full round, provided there is no medial knee pain, swelling or sense of instability afterward. The exact progression also depends substantially on which knee is injured and whether the golfer swings right- or left-handed, because the loading and rotational demands are quite different.
For an uncomplicated Grade 2 MCL, 6–8 weeks to fairly normal athletic function is a reasonable general expectation, although some people progress faster and others take longer. 
Given our earlier discussion about competitive golf and ligament injuries, I can also lay out a specific 6-week Grade 2 MCL rehab program for a golfer, including exercises, sets/reps, cardio and exactly when I would reintroduce putting, chipping, range work and full swings.
6-week protocol for golfer
Absolutely. Assuming this is an isolated Grade 2 MCL tear, the knee is stable enough for nonoperative treatment, and a sports-medicine clinician/PT has cleared progressive weight-bearing, here is a practical 6-week golf-oriented program. The calendar is a guide; pain, swelling and stability determine progression.
Week 1 — Protect, restore motion, maintain muscle
Goal: Reduce pain/swelling, protect the healing MCL, regain normal extension and begin restoring flexion.
Daily
Hinged knee brace for walking if prescribed. 
Weight-bearing as tolerated; crutches until walking without a significant limp. 
Ice/compression 15–20 min, particularly after exercise. 
Heel slides: 2 × 15 
Quad sets: 3 × 10, 5-sec holds 
Straight-leg raises: 3 × 10–15 
Side-lying hip abduction: 3 × 15 
Glute bridges: 3 × 12–15 
Standing calf raises: 3 × 15 
Gentle hamstring/calf stretching. 
Stationary bike 10–15 min, essentially no resistance, once ROM allows comfortable pedaling. 
Golf: Putting only if standing and putting are completely comfortable. No full swing or rotational loading.
Avoid: pivoting, twisting, lateral cutting, deep squatting and anything producing medial-knee pain.
Week 2 — Normalize walking + begin closed-chain strength
Goal: Normal gait, minimal swelling, near-full ROM and begin loading the leg.
Strength 3–4 days/week
Stationary bike: 15–25 min 
Bodyweight squat to ~45–60°: 3 × 12 
Light leg press, comfortable ROM: 3 × 12–15 
Step-ups, 4–6": 3 × 10 each leg 
Bridges: 3 × 15 
Hamstring curls: 3 × 12–15 
Calf raises: 3 × 15–20 
Hip abduction/band work: 3 × 15 
Single-leg balance: 3 × 30 sec 
Golf: Putting → short chipping if completely comfortable. Start with perhaps 20–30 balls, focusing on upper-body technique rather than aggressive lower-body rotation.
Progress when: normal walking, little/no swelling and exercises don't produce increased medial-knee pain the following day.
Week 3 — Build strength and single-leg control
This is where I would start treating the leg more like an athlete again.
Strength 3 days/week
Bike/elliptical: 20–30 min 
Squat: 3 × 10–12 
Leg press: 3 × 10–12 
Step-ups: 3 × 10 
Controlled step-downs: 3 × 8–10 
Split squat, shallow initially: 3 × 8–10 
Romanian deadlift: 3 × 10 
Hamstring curl: 3 × 10–12 
Calf raise: 3 × 15 
Hip/glute strengthening: 3 × 12–15 
Single-leg balance + reach: 3 rounds 
The major coaching point is excellent knee alignment—don't allow the knee to collapse inward and load the healing MCL.
Golf: Putting/chipping unrestricted if symptom-free. Add 30–50% swings with wedges and short irons. Start with ~20 balls and build toward 40–50.
Still no aggressive driver swings.
Week 4 — Strength + controlled rotation
Goal: Restore substantial leg strength and begin preparing the knee for rotational forces.
Strength 3 days/week
Squat: 3–4 × 8–10 
Leg press: 3–4 × 8–10 
Split squat: 3 × 8–10 
Step-down: 3 × 10 
RDL: 3 × 8–10 
Single-leg leg press: 3 × 10 
Hamstring curl: 3 × 10 
Calf raises: 3 × 15 
Lateral band walks: 3 × 10–15 steps each direction 
Single-leg balance with controlled trunk rotation. 
Cardio: bike/elliptical 25–35 min.
If the knee has full ROM, essentially no swelling and good single-leg control, introduce brisk walking → short straight-line jogging intervals if desired. Running isn't necessary for golf, however, so I wouldn't make running a prerequisite.
Golf: Progress from ½ swings → ¾ swings, wedges through mid-irons. Gradually increase rotation and weight transfer. Consider hitting from a tee initially to reduce ground interaction.
Week 5 — Athletic strength + golf-specific loading
Goal: Make the knee tolerate forces greater than those it will ordinarily encounter during golf.
Strength 3 days/week
Squat: 3 × 6–10 
Leg press: 3 × 8–10 
Bulgarian/split squat: 3 × 8 
Single-leg RDL: 3 × 8–10 
Step-down: 3 × 10 
Hamstring curl: 3 × 10 
Lateral band walks: 3 sets 
Single-leg balance with rotation: 3 sets 
Begin controlled dynamic work:
Small lateral steps 
Controlled lateral lunges—only if completely pain-free 
Low-level hops 
Forward/backward movement 
Gradually faster rotational drills 
Golf: Progress to 75–90% swings, longer irons → hybrids/fairway woods → driver.
A sample range session might be:
10 chips → 10 wedges → 10 short irons → 10 mid-irons → 5–10 woods → 5 drivers.
The knee should remain comfortable during the session and later that day/the following morning.
Week 6 — Return to golf
Goal: Demonstrate that the knee can tolerate normal golf without a reaction.
Strength continues 2–3×/week, now approaching normal training loads.
Add more challenging:
Single-leg squat 
Loaded split squat 
Single-leg RDL 
Lateral lunge 
Balance + rotation 
Controlled hopping/agility if appropriate 
Golf progression:
Full range session → 9 holes with cart → 18 holes with cart → 9 holes walking → eventually 18 holes walking.
Full swings can progress toward 100% speed.
I would initially avoid hitting huge buckets of balls. Fifty quality swings with no symptoms tells you more than hitting 150 balls and discovering that evening that the MCL was overloaded.
The most important rule
Use a 24-hour response test. A little discomfort during rehabilitation isn't necessarily a problem, but the knee should be back to baseline by the following morning.
If an exercise or golf session causes increased medial pain, swelling, limping or instability that persists into the next day, reduce the previous workload by roughly 25–50% rather than continuing to progress.
By the end of Week 6, I'd want to see full ROM, no meaningful swelling, no giving-way, pain-free walking/stairs, strong single-leg squat/step-down mechanics, and ideally ≥90% strength/function versus the uninvolved leg before unrestricted sports activity.
One additional point for golf: which knee has the Grade 2 MCL injury and whether the golfer is right- or left-handed matters quite a bit. If you tell me right or left knee + right- or left-handed golfer, I can modify Weeks 3–6 specifically around the forces that knee experiences during the backswing and downswing.

Hey [CUSTOMER],
Sorry for the delay but here is an oral GH secretagogue you asked about. See below for all info I summarized, knowing that results vary but anecdotal evidence favors some efficiency. I also put a place you can get it if you desire, because our 3rd party partner deals mainly with injectables at this point.
Call me if you have any questions. And of course you can do your own research to see if it makes sense for you or someone in your orbit to use.
Have a great day!
Ibutamoren (MK-677) Oral non-peptide* GH stimulant
Primary use: to increase the body’s natural growth hormone and IGF-1 levels to support muscle growth, recovery, and overall anabolic function without injections
Mechanism: mimics ghrelin (“hunger hormone”) to activate ghrelin receptors (GHS-R1a), which signals the hypothalamus & pituitary to increase natural GH pulse release; liver then produces more IGF-1 leading to an increase in protein synthesis and reduction in muscle breakdown
Typical dosing used in research and practice is ~10–25 mg once daily, usually taken in the evening (or split), with many starting at ~10 mg to assess tolerance and adjusting based on response
Notes: MK-677 is an oral compound that increases your body’s growth hormone by mimicking a hunger signal. That can help with recovery, muscle maintenance, and sleep—but it also makes you hungrier and can affect blood sugar, so it’s not a shortcut unless everything else is dialed in and human results vary and largely based on anecdotes. MK-677 is not FDA Approved and classified as a research compound.
*1 Ibutamoren (MK-677) is a small-molecule, non-peptide compound, specifically an orally active ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist. It’s a synthetic, drug-like molecule (not a chain of amino acids like peptides designed to bind the ghrelin receptor and stimulate GH release. Its small-molecule structure is what allows it to be taken orally and remain stable in the body. Therefore MK-677 works like a drug, not a peptide—so you can take it orally and it still activates the GH pathway effectively
Our peptide/GLP-1 3rd party partner does not carry MK-677 - so see below.

source_file: 2026/Magtein magnisium supp.docx
filename: Magtein magnisium supp
expert_section:
In 2 grams (2000 mg) of Magtein (Magnesium L-Threonate), you'll find approximately 144 to 145 mg of elemental magnesium, as Magtein is about 7.2% elemental magnesium by weight, with most brands providing around 144-145mg per 2g dose for brain health support. 
Here's the breakdown:
Magtein (Magnesium L-Threonate): A specific compound designed to cross the blood-brain barrier.
Elemental Magnesium: The actual magnesium mineral content.
Calculation: A 2000 mg serving of Magtein typically yields about 144-145 mg of elemental magnesium (2000 mg * ~0.072 = ~144 mg). 
Always check your supplement's label for the exact elemental magnesium amount, as it's the crucial figure for your daily intake. 
 2-gram (2000 mg) serving of a Magtein (magnesium L-threonate) supplement generally provides 144 mg to 147 mg of elemental magnesium. This amount accounts for about 7% to 8% of the total weight of the magnesium L-threonate compound. 
The remaining weight in the 2 grams of magnesium L-threonate is primarily the L-threonate molecule, a water-soluble substance derived from the metabolic breakdown of vitamin C. 
If the product is in capsule or powder form, other inactive ingredients are also present, which vary by manufacturer. Common "other ingredients" found in Magtein supplements include: 
Hypromellose (cellulose capsule)
Rice flour
Stearic acid (vegetable source)
Silicon dioxide
Cellulose
Magnesium stearate 
These ingredients function as fillers, anti-caking agents, or make up the capsule itself, ensuring the product can be manufactured and consumed easily.

expert_section:
As far as the creatine thing below - it doesn't matter that it is not 100% dissolved when you ingest it. In fact, you can eat it straight out of the container in the evidence-based monohydrate form, and it will work just as well because your digestive tract creates the necessary solubility factor.
See below for a question on the new "water soluble creatine" products being promoted - total marketing.
Q: 
What is the insoluble residue in the Creatine Monohydrate?  One level measuring cup in 8-10 oz of water does not fully dissolve, leaving clear crystals.  I've tried using hot water and letting the solution stand for a while -- same thing. The crystals are tasteless, so I guess they are not the flavoring and sweetener.  
Water soluble or micronized creatine
Takeaway:
Our professionals deliver the only proven, science-backed creatine monohydrate and would not offer an alternative source because of the lack of evidence to date that any form is better, including solubility. Creatine does not have to totally dissolve in water (or fluid mix) before you ingest it. Your digestive tract takes care of preparing any creatine (from your food, or supplements) for proper absorption once it enters the body regardless of its solubility.  
More info 
The sales numbers or marketing claims for “water soluble creatine” or micronized creatine, although the form means nothing related to efficacy, is simply a product of the hype around creatine and influencer money to separate a brand from the norm, – nothing to do with results – just marketing spin.
Creatine supplementation does not have to be “water soluble” or micronized to be safe and effective. In fact, all powdered creatine products are water-dispersible, but they are not all highly water-soluble or need to be. Most powdered creatine monohydrate (CrM) products are considered moderately soluble in water but proven superior to all other creatine forms including the advertised “water soluble” or micronized creatine products. Creatine supplementation does not need to be “water soluble” or micronized for the body to use it. The body (GI tract) dissolves the ingested creatine and puts into solution to absorb it.
The evidence-based scientific position including The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand on creatine states:
Creatine Monohydrate is the most extensively studied and clinically effective form. Claims that other forms deliver greater uptake or are superior are currently unfounded – basically a marketing spin to help justify their increase in costs – in other words the other forms (“water soluble”/micronized ) are more expensive with no efficacy advantage. 
End all be all by science:
Creatine monohydrate is the better-supported formula.
Many “water-soluble creatines” dissolve more easily (salts like citrate/malate/HCl), but the key metrics are muscle creatine loading and performance outcomes. And the best head-to-head evidence shows no superiority vs monohydrate (and sometimes worse, as with ethyl ester), not to mention more expensive.
Your business solution is the 3 creatine monohydrate products supported by the strongest science sold separately or in multi-ingredient formulas containing other proven ergogenic aids/ingredients and included in layered performance stacks.
What They Are
Creatine Monohydrate
The classic, original form of creatine used in research and supplements.
Very simple molecule: creatine bound to a water molecule.
Most studied form of creatine in the history of sports science.
“Water-Soluble Creatine”
A marketing term not tied to a single chemical structure.
Usually refers to:
Creatine salts (e.g., creatine citrate, creatine malate)
Creatine that’s been processed to be more soluble in water
Other proprietary forms claiming better dissolution/absorption
❗️Important: “Water-soluble” does not define the chemistry — it’s usually just a way to say “dissolves better in water.”
🧠 Key Differences
| Feature | Creatine Monohydrate | “Water-Soluble Creatine” Forms |
| Scientific backing | Extensive, strong | Very limited |
| Absorption into muscle | Proven effective | Often inferred, not proven * |
| Solubility in water | Moderate | Higher (by chemistry) |
| Effectiveness for performance | Established | Not consistently superior |
| Typical cost | Lower | Usually higher |
| Side effects (bloating, digestive issues) | Sometimes reported | Backbone data lacking |
* Better solubility ≠ better performance or uptake — it just means it dissolves more easily in your drink.
What the Science Says
Creatine Monohydrate
✔️ Most studied form — with hundreds of trials showing:
Increases strength and power
Increases lean mass
Improves muscle creatine stores
Enhances performance in high-intensity exercise
Safe with long-term use in healthy adults
→ Gold standard in research. This form is the benchmark against which all other creatines are judged.
Water-Soluble / Alternate Forms
Some show slightly better solubility in water
But usually do not show better muscle uptake or performance compared to monohydrate
Evidence that they’re superior is either weak, uncontrolled, or manufacturer-funded
In direct comparisons, creatine monohydrate consistently matches or beats other forms for increasing muscle creatine and improving performance.
Many studies conclude:
If a creatine form doesn’t outperform monohydrate in muscle uptake and performance, then solubility alone isn’t meaningful for effectiveness.
So Which Is Better?
Winner: Creatine Monohydrate
✔️ Better supported by science
✔️ Proven to increase muscle creatine levels
✔️ Shows real improvements in strength, power, and body composition
✔️ Widely used in clinical and sports studies
✔️ Excellent safety profile and cost-effective
Even when other forms are marketed as “water-soluble” or “faster-absorbing,” they haven’t been shown to deliver better results than monohydrate in real performance outcomes.
📌 A Note on Solubility & Side Effects
Some people think “water-soluble = better absorbed = fewer stomach issues.”
In reality:
Poor solubility may make monohydrate feel gritty, but that doesn’t reduce effectiveness.
Micronized monohydrate (smaller particle size) dissolves better in water and is essentially monohydrate — it often reduces gastric discomfort without changing outcomes.
True side effects (rare) are usually unrelated to solubility.
Bottom Line
🔹 Creatine Monohydrate = the best-proven choice.
It’s the science-backed standard for strength and performance.
🔹 “Water-soluble creatine” may mix better, but it’s not proven to be more effective at increasing muscle creatine or enhancing performance.
Comparisons 
Here’s a summary of key scientific research comparing creatine monohydrate with other “water-soluble” or alternative creatine forms, so you can see what actual studies show — not just marketing claims:
🧪 1. Creatine Monohydrate is the Most Studied and Effective
Creatine monohydrate has been the standard form used in most clinical and sports nutrition research for decades, with a strong body of evidence supporting its ability to increase muscle creatine stores, strength, and high-intensity exercise performance. 
Reviews of the literature consistently conclude that other forms do not outperform creatine monohydrate in terms of muscle uptake or performance benefits. 
One authoritative review states there are no data showing any alternative creatine significantly increases muscle creatine storage more than monohydrate when taken in equal creatine amounts. 
🧪 2. Alternative Forms (e.g., Creatine HCl, Salts) — Mixed or Insufficient Evidence
Some alternative forms like creatine hydrochloride (HCl) and certain creatine salts claim higher solubility or potential absorption advantages. 
A few small studies suggest creatine HCl might dissolve better or reduce water retention in some users, but they do not show clear superiority for performance gains over monohydrate. 
In rare isolated studies, some performance measures improved with alternative creatine types, but differences vs monohydrate were generally small, inconsistent, or not statistically superior. 
Many alternative forms have limited published, peer-reviewed research — so claims of “better absorption” aren’t well backed by robust human trials. 
🧪 3. Systematic Reviews Back Monohydrate
A systematic review specifically looking at all alternative creatine types found they were effective as ergogenic aids, but none consistently outperformed creatine monohydrate for strength, hypertrophy, or performance. 
Another recent publication reiterated that monohydrate remains the preferred and recommended form because most evidence supports it — whereas other forms “require further scientific investigation” before being recommended instead. 
🧪 4. Solubility ≠ Superior Performance
Some alternative forms do dissolve better in water or may be marketed as “more bioavailable,” but greater solubility does not automatically translate to better muscle creatine uptake or performance improvements in controlled studies. 
The body regulates creatine uptake into muscle using a transporter system (SLC6A8), and simply changing creatine’s water solubility generally doesn’t bypass this physiological mechanism. 
📌 Practical Takeaways from the Research
✅ Creatine Monohydrate
Most evidence for increasing muscle creatine levels and improving strength, power, and performance. 
Well-studied in athletes and non-athletes. 
Proven safe and cost-effective. 
⛔ Other Forms (HCl, salts, buffered, citrate, etc.)
Some dissolve more easily or may feel gentler on the stomach, but do not consistently show stronger performance benefits than monohydrate. 
Research is limited and often small or preliminary. 
🧠 Summary
✔️ Creatine monohydrate is the gold-standard, most science-backed form for boosting muscle creatine, strength, and performance.
✔️ “Water-soluble” or alternative creatine forms do not have strong evidence showing they’re better than monohydrate, even if they dissolve easier.
✔️ Solubility or marketing claims alone don’t make a creatine form superior.
If you want, I can break down specific studies (e.g., sample sizes, protocols, outcomes) that directly compared creatine monohydrate with popular alternatives like creatine HCl or other salts
Thought for 8s
Below are specific head-to-head studies (and major position stands) that directly address “water-soluble”/alternative creatines vs creatine monohydrate (CrM).
Best direct comparison studies
1) Creatine HCl vs Creatine Monohydrate (recent RCT, athletes)
Design: Placebo-controlled randomized trial in team-sport athletes comparing CrM vs creatine HCl (Cr-HCl) at low doses.
Finding: Similar effects on neuromuscular/strength outcomes; no evidence Cr-HCl outperforms CrM. 
A separate 2024 paper likewise found Cr-HCl did not show benefit over CrM when combined with resistance training. 
Takeaway: If “water-soluble creatine” = creatine HCl, the best current human trials show no meaningful advantage over monohydrate.
2) Creatine Ethyl Ester vs Creatine Monohydrate (classic study)
Design: Resistance-training study comparing creatine ethyl ester (CEE) vs CrM.
Finding: CEE was worse—it was not as effective at increasing muscle creatine and did not improve body composition/strength/power as well as CrM. 
Takeaway: One of the clearest “alternative form” losses to monohydrate.
3) “Buffered creatine” (Kre-Alkalyn–type) vs Creatine Monohydrate
Design: Double-blind trial in resistance-trained individuals comparing buffered creatine vs CrM (and different doses).
Finding: Buffered creatine did not produce greater increases in muscle creatine, body composition, or training adaptations than CrM. 
Takeaway: “Buffered” claims (less breakdown, better results at lower dose) are not supported in controlled human data.
What the major scientific position stands say (big picture)
The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand states:
CrM is the most extensively studied and clinically effective form. 
Claims that other forms deliver greater uptake or are superior are currently unfounded – basically marketing spin to help increase costs
The other forms (“water soluble”) are more expensive with no adbvantage. 
So… which is “better” by science?
Creatine monohydrate is the better-supported formula.
Many “water-soluble creatines” dissolve more easily (salts like citrate/malate/HCl), but the key question is muscle creatine loading + performance outcomes—and the best head-to-head evidence shows no consistent superiority vs monohydrate (and sometimes worse, as with ethyl ester). 
Practical recommendation (what I’d tell a trainer/client)
Choose creatine monohydrate (ideally micronized for mixability).
Dose: 3–5 g daily (no cycling required for most people).
If someone gets GI upset: split dose (e.g., 2 g + 2 g) and take with a meal; the “fix” is usually dosing/mixing, not switching to a pricier “water-soluble” form.
Q: is all creatine supplementation in powdered form water soluble including creatine monohydrate?
Short answer: No.
All powdered creatine products are water-dispersible, but they are not all highly water-soluble — and creatine monohydrate is only moderately soluble in water.
Let’s break that down clearly.
What “Water-Soluble” Actually Means
Water-soluble = dissolves completely in water at a meaningful concentration.
There’s a difference between:
Soluble → dissolves at the molecular level
Dispersible → suspends/mixes but doesn’t fully dissolve
Most creatine powders will mix into water, but that does not mean they are highly soluble.
Creatine Monohydrate (CrM)
Moderate solubility
About 14–18 g per liter at room temperature
Leaves sediment if not stirred
Dissolves better in warm water
“Micronized” versions dissolve more easily (smaller particle size)
Important:
Even if some powder settles at the bottom, absorption is not impaired once it reaches the stomach. Solubility in the glass does not equal absorption in the body.
Other Creatine Forms (Often Marketed as “Water-Soluble”)
Some forms are chemically modified to increase solubility:
| Form | Solubility vs Monohydrate |
| Creatine HCl | Much higher |
| Creatine Citrate | Higher |
| Creatine Nitrate | Higher |
| Buffered Creatine | Slightly higher |
These dissolve more easily in water, but higher solubility has not been shown to improve muscle creatine uptake or performance compared to monohydrate.
Key Physiological Reality
Creatine absorption depends primarily on:
Intestinal transport
The creatine transporter (SLC6A8)
Muscle saturation levels
It does not depend heavily on how clear your drink looks.
Once in solution in stomach acid, creatine monohydrate becomes fully available for absorption.
Bottom Line
All creatine powders will mix with water.
Creatine monohydrate is not highly water-soluble, but it is sufficiently soluble for full effectiveness.
Other forms may dissolve better, but they are not proven to work better.
Solubility is mostly a convenience/texture issue, not a performance issue.

MK-677, also known as Ibutamoren, is a “growth hormone secretagogue,” a substance that stimulates the production of growth hormone. It is not approved for human use, which makes it an unapproved drug. It is also not legal for use as an ingredient in dietary supplements or any other consumer or commercial products. It can only be used for research purposes.
MK-677 is on the DoD Prohibited Dietary Supplement Ingredients List and the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List. It is not legal for use.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has posted warning letters to companies illegally selling products containing MK-677. These types of products are sometimes labeled as dietary supplements with a “Supplement Facts” label, as a research chemical with a “Research Facts” label, or even labeled as “For Research Use Only.”
Even though it is illegal, MK-677 is currently marketed with claims to help build muscle or increase muscle mass, decrease body fat, and increase energy. In addition, products that contain MK-677 are often combined with SARMs (or even indicate MK-677 as a SARM). SARMs are also illegal and prohibited for use.
What are the safety concerns?
A number of health risks have been associated with the use of MK-677 (Ibutamoren).
FDA lists Ibutamoren as an ingredient that “…poses significant safety risks due to the potential for congestive heart failure in certain patients.” A clinical trial was stopped early due to concerns that Ibutamoren may increase the rate of heart failure.
Ibutamoren is listed in the Australian Poisons Standard. The long-term safety is not established and the potential adverse effects “…may include those associated with the administration of growth hormones and the potential for downstream health effects such as cardiovascular and hormonal effects.”

Not only is use of MK-677 a health risk, but it could adversely affect a career.
MK-677 is prohibited for use in the military and is on the DoD Prohibited Dietary Supplement Ingredients List and the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List. Therefore, Service Members should not use any products with this ingredient.

Key Legal and Safety Facts
Approved Usage: FDA-approved to treat methemoglobinemia -rare, life-threatening blood disorder where the iron in hemoglobin is oxidized, preventing it from releasing oxygen to body tissues and used in hospitals for conditions like cyanide poisoning.
Unregulated Supplements: Many methylene blue products sold online as "supplements" for energy or brain health are not evaluated or approved by the FDA for safety or purity
Legal Status: It is legal for medical, laboratory, and industrial use. However, using unregulated, non-pharmaceutical-grade forms for self-treatment is risky.

Always consult a healthcare provider, as, unregulated products may contain dangerous impurities
Methylene blue: a controversial diagnostic acid and medication?
The toxic effects of the application of MB are dose-dependent and include serious symptoms such as hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, nausea and vomitus, chest pain, dyspnoea, and hypertension. Some countries regard MB as harmful because of the resulting skin irritation and triggering of an adverse inflammatory response. MB induced serotoninergic toxicity clinically manifests as neuromuscular hyperactivity
Is Methylene Blue A True Brain Booster? A Pharmacologist Explains
Methylene blue is a synthetic dye that exists as a dark green powder and takes on a deep blue color when dissolved in water. My work and that of others suggest that many synthetic dyes widely used in foods and medicines can trigger potentially harmful immune system reactions in the body. But unlike commonly used food dyes – one of which was recently banned by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration – methylene blue is not derived from petroleum, also known as crude oil. Instead, it comes from a different family of dyes, which isn’t thought to have these health concerns.
Methylene blue was first synthesized in 1876 as a dye for textiles and was valued for its intense color and ability to bind well to fabrics. Soon after, German physician Paul Ehrlich discovered its ability to stain biological tissues and to kill the parasite that causes malaria — making it one of the first synthetic drugs used in medicine.
The chemical didn’t gain widespread use as a malaria treatment because it was no more effective than quinine, the standard therapy at the time. But in the 1930s, the dye found a new use in testing the safety of raw or unpasteurized milk. If its blue color faded quickly, the milk was contaminated with bacteria, but if it remained blue, the milk was considered relatively clean.
This safety test now is largely obsolete. But it works thanks to methylene blue’s chemical superpower, which is that its molecules can swap electrons with other molecules, like a tiny battery charger.
How Do Doctors Use It Today?
That same chemical superpower enables some of methylene blue’s medical uses. Most significantly, doctors use it to treat a rare blood disorder called methemoglobinemia, in which hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, takes on a different form that can’t do the job. Methylene blue restores hemoglobin’s function by transferring an electron.
Doctors also sometimes use methylene blue to treat the effects of carbon monoxide poisoning, septic shock or toxicities from drugs such as chemotherapy. It is also used as a surgical dye to highlight specific tissues such as lymph nodes, or to identify where tissue is leaky and therefore may be damaged.
How Does Methylene Blue Affect The Brain?
Methylene blue can enter the brain by crossing the protective tissue barrier that surrounds it. Researchers have also found that the chemical can protect and support mitochondria, cell structures that are often described as the powerhouses of the cell. Methylene blue may help mitochondria generate energy for cells to use. For these reasons, researchers are studying methylene blue’s effect on the brain.
So far, most of what’s known about the substance’s effects on the brain comes from studies in rats and in cells grown in a lab dish – not in people. For example, researchers have found that methylene blue may improve learning, boost memory and protect brain cells in rats with a condition that mimics Alzheimer’s disease.
Is Methylene Blue Safe?
Methylene blue is generally safe when used under medical supervision. However, the chemical has some serious risks.
For one thing, it can interact with widely used medications. Methylene blue inhibits a molecule called monoamine oxidase, whose job is to break down an important brain chemical, serotonin. Many commonly used medications for treating anxiety and depression target serotonin. Taking the supplement along with these medicines can cause a condition called serotonin syndrome, which can lead to agitation, confusion, high fever, rapid heart rate, muscle stiffness and, in severe cases, seizures or even death.
In people with a rare genetic deficiency of an enzyme called G6PD, methylene blue can cause a dangerous condition in which red blood cells break down too quickly. At high doses, the chemical can also raise blood pressure or cause heart problems. Also, it’s considered unsafe for pregnant or breastfeeding women because it may harm the fetus or baby.
Overall, while scientists have found hints of some fascinating properties of methylene blue, much larger, longer trials are needed to know if it truly works, what the right dose is and how safe it is over time.
Lorne J. Hofseth, Professor and Associate Dean for Research, College of Pharmacy,

1 teaspoon sea salt (~5–6 grams) → ~2,000–2,300 mg sodium
Essentially the entire recommended daily limit for many adults.
For reference:
General guidance: ~2,300 mg sodium/day max (many health organizations)
Optimal for blood pressure-sensitive individuals: ~1,500 mg/day

To obtain only meaningful magnesium from sea salt, you'd exceed safe sodium intake very quickly.
Q: is taking Sea salt for minerals as sufficient as a taking a complete multivitamin a mineral formula with the amounts listed on the label and 3rd party tested. And when taking Sea salt for minerals, are the amounts of each mineral listed on the product label? and how much sodium is generally in a dose of sea salt.
A: Short answer: No — sea salt is not nutritionally equivalent to a complete multivitamin/mineral (MVM).
And no — most sea salt labels do not list meaningful amounts of trace minerals beyond sodium.
Let’s break this down clearly.
1. Is Sea Salt Equal to a Complete Multivitamin/Mineral?
Sea Salt
Sea salt is:
~97–99% sodium chloride and small, variable trace amounts of:
Magnesium; Potassium; Calcium; Iron; Zinc; Iodine (usually very little unless fortified)
These trace minerals are present in tiny, inconsistent amounts — often measured in milligrams or micrograms per several grams of salt. To reach meaningful intake levels of magnesium or potassium from sea salt, you would need to consume dangerously high sodium levels.
Complete Multivitamin & Mineral Formula
A properly formulated MVM:
Lists exact dosages of each vitamin and mineral
Covers common shortfall nutrients (magnesium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc, selenium, etc.)
Is typically 3rd-party tested (NSF, USP, etc.)
Designed to provide clinically relevant doses without excess sodium
An MVM is built to:
Complement modern diets
Provide predictable dosing
Deliver physiologically meaningful amounts
Sea salt is not.
2. Are Trace Minerals Listed on Sea Salt Labels?
Usually no. Most sea salt labels list sodium (mg per serving); Sometimes chloride.
They do not typically list amounts of magnesium, potassium, iron, zinc, iodine (unless iodized).
Why? Because:
Levels are inconsistent and often too low to qualify for meaningful Daily Value listing
Mineral content varies by harvest source and batch
You don’t truly know what you're getting in measurable terms.
3. How Much Sodium Is in Sea Salt?
Sea salt and table salt are nutritionally very similar regarding sodium.
Typical sodium content:
1 teaspoon sea salt (~5–6 grams) → ~2,000–2,300 mg sodium
Essentially the entire recommended daily limit for many adults.
For reference:
General guidance: ~2,300 mg sodium/day max (many health organizations)
Optimal for blood pressure-sensitive individuals: ~1,500 mg/day
So even ½ teaspoon = ~1,000–1,150 mg sodium
To obtain meaningful magnesium from sea salt, you'd exceed safe sodium intake very quickly.
Nutritional Reality Check- Compare:
| Nutrient | Sea Salt | Complete MVM |
| Sodium | High | Usually minimal |
| Magnesium | Trace (very small) | 50–200+ mg |
| Potassium | Trace | Often 50–100+ mg |
| Iodine | Usually minimal unless iodized | 150 mcg (RDA) |
| Vitamin D | None | 800–2000 IU commonly |
| Zinc | Trace | 8–15 mg |
| Selenium | Trace | 55–200 mcg |
Sea salt is primarily a sodium source — not a micronutrient solution.
Science-Based Conclusion
Sea salt:
Adds flavor
Provides sodium and chloride
Contains trivial trace minerals
Does NOT meaningfully cover nutrient gaps
A complete multivitamin/mineral:
Delivers known, labeled, clinically relevant amounts
Helps address common population shortfalls
Is standardized and tested
They serve completely different purposes.
Bottom Line
Sea salt is a sodium seasoning with tiny trace minerals.
A complete MVM is a structured micronutrient support system.
They are not interchangeable.

Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia), or "Malaysian ginseng," is a Southeast Asian root scientifically shown to improve testosterone levels (30–40% in some studies), libido, stress resilience (reduced cortisol), and mood. It is widely used for age-related hormone decline and, with 200–400mg doses, to enhance physical performance, muscle strength, and erectile function.  Popular herbal supplement in the United States, as extracts of tongkat ali roots have been promoted as increasing testosterone levels and improving athletic performance. Reports of clinically apparent liver injury attributed to tongkat ali in body builders have recently appeared.
National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov) +6
Scientific Findings and Key Benefits
Testosterone Boost: Studies indicate it supports higher free and total testosterone by lowering sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and aiding in the release of bound testosterone. It is particularly effective for men with low testosterone or under stress.
Libido and Sexual Health: Known as a traditional aphrodisiac, scientific trials confirm it improves erectile function, libido, and male fertility.
Stress and Mood: Research demonstrates that daily supplementation reduces cortisol (stress hormone) and improves psychological mood states, reducing tension, anger, and confusion.
Physical Performance: It is used by athletes to improve body composition and speed up recovery. 
National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov) +10

Standardization is Key: Clinical benefits are typically associated with standardized extracts of the bioactive compound eurycomanone.
Small Studies: While promising, many studies on humans are small, and more extensive research is required to fully confirm its efficacy compared to conventional, standard medicine.
Safety: It is generally considered safe when used appropriately, but some studies note the potential for high levels of mercury in unrefined products

More Info
Recent studies on Turkesterone, a phytoecdysteroid (500mg/d) show mixed results, with limited, often conflicting evidence in human trials regarding muscle growth and performance improvements. Proposed mechanism is an increase in MUSCLE PROTEIN SYNTHESIS. While some studies suggest it may aid in recovery or provide subtle ergogenic effects, recent 2024-2025 research indicates no significant increases in lean muscle mass, muscle strength, or metabolic rate compared to placebos. Almost all Turkesterone studies are animal and cell studies, with only 3 small human trials. Science consensus: across the board, creatine supplementation alone far outperforms Turkesterone for performance and muscle gain.
Your business solution: All else equal, the 3 different performance/muscle gain bundles we sell, which all include creatine, far surpass the potential gains (if any) compared to Turkesterone supplementation. Further, long-term effects of Turkesterone use are virtually non-existent, leaving its long-term safety profile unknown. Long-term safety and efficacy use of creatine and other bundled evidence-based products is well established.
Key Findings on Turkesterone Studies:
Muscle Growth/Performance: A 2025 study found no significant changes in body composition, strength, or power in participants over 4 weeks. Earlier studies suggested potential, but more robust human research is needed.
Safety & Side Effects:
 Studies show doses up to 2,000 mg are generally well-tolerated with no significant adverse impacts on blood pressure, heart rate, or liver function
. Minor issues like nausea or stomach discomfort may occur
.
Mechanism: As a phytoecdysteroid, it is thought to act on muscle cells through pathways different from traditional steroids, focusing on protein synthesis stimulation rather than androgen receptor binding.
Long-Term Effects: Data on the long-term effects of Turkesterone use is virtually non-existent, leaving its long-term safety profile unknown.
Legality in Sports: It is currently not banned in sports, though similar ecdysteroids are on the WADA monitoring list. 
YouTube +1
Conclusion of Current Research
The majority of studies supporting high efficacy are in animals (rodents) or cell cultures, with human data still in its infancy. Although safe, studies to date fail to definitively support its effectiveness as a potent, natural anabolic agent for muscle growth.
3.5. Turkesterone and Ajuga turkestanica
Turkesterone is a PE, with 27 carbon atoms and seven OH-groups; it is considered that the OH groups at C-20 and C-11 are responsible for the anabolic effects [28,215]. Turkesterone is considered to possess an anabolic effect, and it is used as DS by athletes, instead of anabolic steroids [28,30]. It is found in some endemic plants, such as A. turkestanica, R. carthamoides, Triticum aestivum L., Vitex scabra, etc. [13,69,216,217,218]. The highest content of turkesterone is considered to be in Ajuga turkestanica [19]. Moreover, in DSs, turkesterone is derived from A. turkestanica [28].
Ecdysteroid-enriched preparations of A. turkestanica (or pure turkesterone) exhibit anabolic effects [216,219,220].
Ajuga turkestanica, a plant species of the Lamiaceae family, grows wild in the Boysun mountainous region of Central Asia, Uzbekistan. It is a perennial plant, that normally grows on clay, petrous, and rubbly slopes and rocks, with a height of 40–60 cm [14]. Both the aerial parts and root sections are utilized in folk medicine to prevent obesity, hair loss, and gastrointestinal diseases [14,216].
The phytochemical profile of A. turkestanica has indicated the existence of several biologically active secondary metabolites, such as carbohydrates, iridoids, diterpenes, phytoecdysteroids, flavonoids, sterol glycosides, and phenylethanoid glycosides [14,53,216]. The A. turkestanica extract contained 2.1% (w/w) turkesterone and 0.9% (w/w) 20HE [19]. Other isolated Pes are cyasterone, ajugasterone B, α-ecdysone, ecdysone 2,3-monoacetonide, and 22-acetylcyasterone [59,221,222].
Extracts from A. turkestanica are associated with wound-healing effects [223], as well as antiproliferative, anti-stress and immunostimulating, antimicrobial, and antioxidant effects [12,59].
